1. The frames show a grid of 307 squares, one for each start month from January 1991 to July 2016. Each square compares buying with renting over a ten-year holding period. Light squares mean the buyer came out ahead after ten years. Dark squares mean the renter came out ahead. The headline says the buyer was ahead in about 3 of 4 start months (75.6%). The renter was ahead in 75 of 307. The data sources are listed as FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac rates. The animation is labeled "ILLUSTRATIVE", and it says "US only · history, not a forecast".

2. The grid itself stays fixed. What changes is the highlighting and the labels. In frames 1 and 2, a dark block of renter-ahead months stands out in the middle of the grid, with a few light squares inside it. In frame 3, the "renter ahead: 75 of 307" label appears and the dark block fades or dims. In frames 4 to 6 the dark block is back and the label stays. In frames 5 and 6, a caption appears at the bottom: "counted: interest · tax · insurance · repairs · buying and selling".

3. Historically, once the full costs of owning are counted, buying beat renting over ten years for most start dates (about 76%). Renting won for a minority of start dates, about a quarter. Those renter-ahead months are clustered together in one stretch of the timeline, not scattered. So the result depended on when you started.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might infer that buying has usually paid off over a ten-year horizon, even after the full costs. They might also infer that it isn't guaranteed, because renting won in roughly one in four start months. The "history, not a forecast" note cautions against treating this as a prediction.

5. The advice in 4 is my own conclusion. The picture and text only report the historical split and which costs were counted. They never tell the viewer to buy or rent.
